items.stem: What is the fundamental economic problem?
options: Firms that produce more than consumers want to buy
Unlimited wants but limited resources with which to satisfy them
Prices that are too high for many consumers
A money supply that is too small for the economy
items.answer: Unlimited wants but limited resources with which to satisfy them
items.markingKey: The economic problem: wants are unlimited, resources (land, labour, capital, enterprise) are finite, so choices must be made.

items.stem: Explain why scarcity exists even in high-income economies.
items.answer: Although output per head is high, resources are still finite while wants keep growing as incomes rise, so not every want can be met and choices are still needed.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: resources finite; 1 mark: wants grow/unlimited so choices still required [2]

items.stem: Explain the difference between needs and wants.
items.answer: Needs are goods and services essential for survival, such as food, water and shelter. Wants are desires for goods and services beyond these, such as entertainment; wants are unlimited.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: needs essential for survival with example; 1 mark: wants are desires beyond needs/unlimited [2]

items.stem: In Ostrelia there are 480 social housing units but 600 families on the waiting list. Calculate the shortfall as a percentage of what is wanted.

In Calvania there are 750 school places but 937 children of school age. (a) Calculate the shortfall as a percentage of what is wanted. (b) Explain how these figures illustrate the basic economic problem.
items.answer: (a) 20% (b) Wants exceed the resources available; the resource has alternative uses and cannot satisfy all wants, so a choice must be made.
items.markingKey: (a) 187/937 × 100 = 20% [2] (b) limited resource vs greater wants [1]; choice/allocation needed [1] [2] Total [4]

items.stem: Extract: The government of Dravonia has $600 million for new projects this year. Ministers have proposed a hospital ($300 million), a rail link to Accra ($200 million) and a programme of school building ($150 million), as well as a cut in taxes. Opposition politicians say the government should “stop wasting money and simply do everything”. (a) Calculate how much more than the budget would be needed to fund all three projects. (b) Explain the opportunity cost to the government of choosing the rail link.
items.answer: (a) $50 million (b) The benefits of the next best project that cannot now be funded (e.g. the hospital) are forgone.
items.markingKey: (a) 300 + 200 + 150 = 650; |650 − 600| = 50 [2] (b) 1 mark: next best alternative; 1 mark: applied to extract [2]

items.stem: Explain why the basic economic problem means that every economy must make choices.
items.answer: Because resources are scarce relative to unlimited wants, an economy cannot produce everything people want. It must choose which wants to satisfy, and using resources for one purpose means they cannot be used for another.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: scarce resources vs unlimited wants; 1 mark: cannot satisfy all wants; 1 mark: resources have alternative uses so choice is needed [3]

items.stem: Explain why time can be regarded as a scarce resource.
items.answer: Each person has only 24 hours a day, which has alternative uses such as work, study and leisure; using time for one activity means it cannot be used for another.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: fixed amount of time; 1 mark: alternative uses so choice needed [2]

items.stem: In Quentara there are 520 school places but 650 children of school age. Calculate the shortfall as a percentage of what is wanted.
Orchid Ltd has one factory in Lima and orders for both televisions and electric scooters that exceed what it can produce. Explain how the basic economic problem applies to Orchid Ltd.
items.answer: The factory’s capacity (machines, workers, time) is limited while orders are greater, so Orchid Ltd must choose which product to make and in what quantity.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: limited capacity/resources; 1 mark: demand exceeds capacity; 1 mark: choice of what to produce [3]

items.stem: Farmland near Accra can be used for new housing or for growing food. Using the concept of scarcity, explain why the city council must make a choice.
items.answer: Land is a scarce resource with alternative uses; the same land cannot be used for both housing and farming, so the council must decide which want to satisfy and accept giving up the other.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: land is scarce/finite; 1 mark: alternative uses; 1 mark: choice means the other use is given up [3]

items.stem: What is meant by opportunity cost?
options: The cost of producing one more unit of a good
The value of the next best alternative forgone when a choice is made
The total value of all alternatives given up
The money price paid for a good
items.answer: The value of the next best alternative forgone when a choice is made
items.markingKey: Opportunity cost = next best alternative given up, not the sum of all alternatives and not the money price.

items.stem: Explain why a good that is provided free to consumers by the government still has an opportunity cost.
items.answer: Producing it uses scarce resources (labour, materials, capital) that could have been used to produce something else; society gives up that alternative even though the consumer pays nothing.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: uses scarce resources; 1 mark: alternative output forgone by society [2]

items.stem: Explain why the opportunity cost of going to university includes more than the tuition fees.
items.answer: The student also gives up the earnings (and work experience) from a job they could have taken instead; these forgone earnings are often the largest part of the opportunity cost.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: forgone earnings; 1 mark: real alternative given up, not just money spent [2]

items.stem: Hana can work for 5 hours at $8 an hour or attend a volunteering day, which is free. Hana attends a volunteering day. Calculate the opportunity cost in money terms.
items.markingKey: Forgone wages $8 × 5 = $40 = $40.

items.stem: Ana values three ways of spending Saturday: a football coaching job (worth $90 to Ana); a part-time job (worth $120 to Ana); a computer course (worth $60 to Ana). Ana makes the rational choice. (a) Identify the choice made and calculate its opportunity cost. (b) Explain why the opportunity cost is not $150.
items.answer: (a) a part-time job; opportunity cost = a football coaching job, worth $90. (b) Only the next best alternative is forgone; Ana could not have done both of the others at once.
items.markingKey: (a) highest value option chosen [1]; opportunity cost = next best, $90 [1] [2] (b) only next best alternative counts [1] [1] Total [3]

items.stem: Elena values three ways of spending Saturday: a private tutoring session (worth $140 to Elena); a part-time job (worth $150 to Elena); a weekend trip (worth $60 to Elena). Elena makes the rational choice. (a) Identify the choice made and calculate its opportunity cost. (b) Explain why the opportunity cost is not $200. (c) The value of a private tutoring session rises by $20. Explain how Elena’s choice changes.
items.answer: (a) a part-time job; opportunity cost = a private tutoring session, worth $140. (b) Only the next best alternative is forgone; Elena could not have done both of the others at once. (c) a private tutoring session is now worth $160, more than a part-time job, so Elena switches to it and the opportunity cost becomes a part-time job ($150).
items.markingKey: (a) highest value option chosen [1]; opportunity cost = next best, $140 [1] [2] (b) only next best alternative counts [1] [1] (c) new ranking [1]; new opportunity cost [1] [2] Total [5]

items.stem: Extract: The government of Jovania has $1200 million for new projects this year. Ministers have proposed a hospital ($150 million), a rail link to Colombo ($300 million) and a programme of school building ($250 million), as well as a cut in taxes. Opposition politicians say the government should “stop wasting money and simply do everything”. (a) Calculate how much of the budget would be left if all three projects were funded. (b) Explain the opportunity cost to the government of choosing the rail link.
items.answer: (a) $500 million (b) The benefits of the next best project that cannot now be funded (e.g. the hospital) are forgone.
items.markingKey: (a) 150 + 300 + 250 = 700; |700 − 1200| = 500 [2] (b) 1 mark: next best alternative; 1 mark: applied to extract [2]

items.stem: Extract: The government of Marvona has $400 million for new projects this year. Ministers have proposed a hospital ($200 million), a rail link to Hanoi ($150 million) and a programme of school building ($350 million), as well as a cut in taxes. Opposition politicians say the government should “stop wasting money and simply do everything”. (a) Using the extract, explain the meaning of the basic economic problem. (b) Explain why the opposition’s suggestion to “do everything” does not solve the economic problem.
items.answer: (a) Limited resources (a budget of $400 million) but many competing wants (hospital, rail, schools, tax cuts), so choices must be made. (b) Borrowing or taxing more still uses scarce resources; resources diverted from private uses or future spending have an opportunity cost.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark: limited resources; 1 mark: unlimited/competing wants; 1 mark: use of extract [3] (b) 1 mark: resources still finite; 1 mark: cost moves elsewhere/future [2]

items.stem: A student chooses to work in a café on Saturday instead of revising or going to a concert. Revising was her second choice. What is the opportunity cost of working?
options: Both the revision and the concert
The wage she earns in the café
items.answer: The revision she gives up
items.markingKey: Opportunity cost is only the next best alternative (revising), not every alternative.

items.stem: Explain how the concept of opportunity cost can help a government decide how to spend its budget.
items.answer: By comparing what is gained from each project with the benefits of the next best project forgone, the government can choose the option whose benefits exceed its opportunity cost.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: identifies alternatives forgone; 1 mark: compare benefit with opportunity cost; 1 mark: choose best use of scarce funds [3]

items.stem: Explain why the opportunity cost of an unemployed worker’s time may be low.
items.answer: An unemployed worker is not currently producing output or earning a wage, so using their time for training or a new job gives up relatively little paid output.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: no current paid work; 1 mark: little forgone so low opportunity cost [2]

items.stem: The council of Hanoi decides to turn a park into a car park. Explain the opportunity cost of this decision.
items.answer: The leisure, environmental and health benefits of the park that are given up by residents are the opportunity cost.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: identifies forgone park benefits; 1 mark: links to next best use of land [2]

items.stem: A farmer in Pelora can use a field to grow either 200 sacks of coffee or 90 tonnes of wheat in a season (or any combination at a constant rate). Calculate the opportunity cost of producing one tonne of wheat.
items.answer: 2.22 sacks of coffee
items.markingKey: 200/90 = 2.22 sacks of coffee per tonne of wheat.

items.stem: A farmer in Fendaria can use a field to grow either 360 tonnes of wheat or 30 bales of cotton in a season (or any combination at a constant rate). (a) Calculate the opportunity cost of one bale of cotton in terms of wheat. (b) Calculate how much wheat is given up if the farmer grows 10 bales of cotton. (c) Explain why the opportunity cost may not stay constant if the farmer uses more fields of differing quality.
items.answer: (a) 12 tonnes of wheat (b) 120 tonnes (c) Land is not equally suited to both crops; as more land switches, less suitable land is used, so more wheat must be given up per extra unit of cotton (increasing opportunity cost).
items.markingKey: (a) 360/30 [1] (b) 10 × 12 = 120 [1] (c) resources not equally suited [1]; increasing opportunity cost [1] [4]

items.stem: A farmer in Lunaria can use a field to grow either 120 tonnes of rice or 90 sacks of coffee in a season (or any combination at a constant rate). (a) Calculate the opportunity cost of one sack of coffee in terms of rice. (b) Calculate how much rice is given up if the farmer grows 15 sacks of coffee. (c) Explain why the opportunity cost may not stay constant if the farmer uses more fields of differing quality.
items.answer: (a) 1.33 tonnes of rice (b) 20 tonnes (c) Land is not equally suited to both crops; as more land switches, less suitable land is used, so more rice must be given up per extra unit of coffee (increasing opportunity cost).
items.markingKey: (a) 120/90 [1] (b) 15 × 1.33 = 20 [1] (c) resources not equally suited [1]; increasing opportunity cost [1] [4]

items.stem: The government of Valdoria must choose between building a new port and expanding free healthcare. Explain, with examples, the concept of opportunity cost and why it is important for decision-makers.
items.answer: Next best alternative forgone; examples for consumers, firms and governments; helps compare options; real cost of resources not money.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: Next best alternative forgone; examples for consumers, firms and governments; helps compare options; real cost of resources not money. Level 3 (6–8): accurate knowledge with a clear, developed analytical chain and, where relevant, an accurate, labelled diagram that is used in the answer; Level 2 (3–5): some correct explanation but undeveloped or partly inaccurate; Level 1 (1–2): limited knowledge, mostly assertion [8]

items.stem: Which are the three main economic agents in a closed economy?
items.answer: Households, firms and the government
items.markingKey: Economic agents are decision-makers: households (consumers/workers), firms (producers) and government.

items.stem: Which question is about how to produce?
options: Should cars be built using robots or skilled workers?
Should more cars or more buses be built?
Should cars be sold to people with the highest incomes?
items.answer: Should cars be built using robots or skilled workers?
items.markingKey: How to produce = choice of production methods/factor combinations.

items.stem: Explain the meaning of the question “what to produce?” and why it arises.
items.answer: It concerns which goods and services, and how much of each, an economy should make with its scarce resources; it arises because resources cannot produce everything wanted.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: which goods and quantities; 1 mark: arises from scarcity [2]

items.stem: The state planning office of Nordavia sets targets for steel and tractor output for next year. Which basic economic question is being answered?
items.answer: What to produce
items.markingKey: What to produce: the targets decide which goods are produced and in what quantities.

items.stem: Extract: The government of Tarvia has $1200 million for new projects this year. Ministers have proposed a hospital ($350 million), a rail link to Istanbul ($200 million) and a programme of school building ($250 million), as well as a cut in taxes. Opposition politicians say the government should “stop wasting money and simply do everything”. (a) Calculate how much of the budget would be left if all three projects were funded. (b) Explain the opportunity cost to the government of choosing the rail link.
items.answer: (a) $400 million (b) The benefits of the next best project that cannot now be funded (e.g. the hospital) are forgone.
items.markingKey: (a) 350 + 200 + 250 = 800; |800 − 1200| = 400 [2] (b) 1 mark: next best alternative; 1 mark: applied to extract [2]

items.stem: Explain the different objectives that households, firms and the government are assumed to pursue.
items.answer: Households aim to maximise utility (satisfaction) from consumption; firms aim to maximise profit; government aims to maximise the welfare of society as a whole.
items.markingKey: 1 mark each agent correctly linked to objective [3]

items.stem: Extract: The government of Marvona has $600 million for new projects this year. Ministers have proposed a hospital ($300 million), a rail link to Nairobi ($250 million) and a programme of school building ($200 million), as well as a cut in taxes. Opposition politicians say the government should “stop wasting money and simply do everything”. (a) Explain the opportunity cost to the government of choosing the rail link. (b) Explain why the opposition’s suggestion to “do everything” does not solve the economic problem.
items.answer: (a) The benefits of the next best project that cannot now be funded (e.g. the hospital) are forgone. (b) Borrowing or taxing more still uses scarce resources; resources diverted from private uses or future spending have an opportunity cost.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark: next best alternative; 1 mark: applied to extract [2] (b) 1 mark: resources still finite; 1 mark: cost moves elsewhere/future [2]

items.stem: Extract: The government of Nordavia has $800 million for new projects this year. Ministers have proposed a hospital ($250 million), a rail link to Cape Town ($350 million) and a programme of school building ($200 million), as well as a cut in taxes. Opposition politicians say the government should “stop wasting money and simply do everything”. (a) Calculate how much of the budget would be left if all three projects were funded. (b) Explain the opportunity cost to the government of choosing the rail link. (c) Explain why the opposition’s suggestion to “do everything” does not solve the economic problem.
items.answer: (a) $0 million (b) The benefits of the next best project that cannot now be funded (e.g. the hospital) are forgone. (c) Borrowing or taxing more still uses scarce resources; resources diverted from private uses or future spending have an opportunity cost.
items.markingKey: (a) 250 + 350 + 200 = 800; |800 − 800| = 0 [2] (b) 1 mark: next best alternative; 1 mark: applied to extract [2] (c) 1 mark: resources still finite; 1 mark: cost moves elsewhere/future [2]

items.stem: What is meant by scarcity in economics?
options: The general level of prices is rising
Goods are temporarily unavailable in shops
A resource has been used up completely
Resources are limited in relation to the wants they could be used to satisfy
items.answer: Resources are limited in relation to the wants they could be used to satisfy
items.markingKey: Scarcity is relative: resources are insufficient to satisfy all wants, not necessarily absent.

items.stem: Chloe has a fixed weekly allowance and wants to buy concert tickets, printed newspapers and save for a new phone. Explain why Chloe faces the problem of scarcity.
items.answer: The allowance is limited while Chloe’s wants exceed what it can buy, so Chloe cannot have everything and must choose between the alternatives.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: limited income/resources; 1 mark: wants exceed means so choice required [2]

items.stem: The government of Rovania has a fixed budget but faces demands for more hospitals, schools and roads. Explain how this illustrates the basic economic problem.
items.answer: The government’s resources (its budget) are limited, while the demands on them are effectively unlimited, so it must choose which projects to fund and which to go without.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: limited budget/resources; 1 mark: unlimited demands so choices must be made [2]

items.stem: In Kestria there are 900 litres of water a day (millions) but 1440 litres demanded a day (millions). Calculate the shortfall as a percentage of what is wanted.
Farmland near Seoul can be used for new housing or for growing food. Using the concept of scarcity, explain why the city council must make a choice.
items.answer: Land is a scarce resource with alternative uses; the same land cannot be used for both housing and farming, so the council must decide which want to satisfy and accept giving up the other.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: land is scarce/finite; 1 mark: alternative uses; 1 mark: choice means the other use is given up [3]

items.stem: Calvania has grown rapidly for twenty years, yet many families still say they cannot afford everything they want. Explain why scarcity is described as the fundamental economic problem and why it requires all economies to make choices.
items.answer: Unlimited wants vs finite resources (land, labour, capital, enterprise); resources have alternative uses; choice and opportunity cost; the three basic questions follow.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: Unlimited wants vs finite resources (land, labour, capital, enterprise); resources have alternative uses; choice and opportunity cost; the three basic questions follow. Level 3 (6–8): accurate knowledge with a clear, developed analytical chain and, where relevant, an accurate, labelled diagram that is used in the answer; Level 2 (3–5): some correct explanation but undeveloped or partly inaccurate; Level 1 (1–2): limited knowledge, mostly assertion [8]

items.stem: A government spends $500 million on a new airport rather than on schools, its next best option. What is the opportunity cost of the airport?
options: The taxes needed to finance it
The flights that will use the airport
The schools that could have been built
items.answer: The schools that could have been built
items.markingKey: The forgone next best use of the resources.

items.stem: Lumen Ltd uses its factory to make washing machines instead of paper. Explain the opportunity cost to Lumen Ltd.
items.answer: The profit (or output) from making paper, the next best use of the factory, is given up.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: forgone output/profit of laptops; 1 mark: next best use of the resources [2]

items.stem: Felix has one evening free and can either work an extra shift, revise for an economics test or go to the cinema. Explain what determines the opportunity cost of revising.
items.answer: It is the value of whichever of the other two options Felix ranks next best (the shift or the cinema), not both of them.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: next best alternative; 1 mark: only one alternative, not all [2]

items.stem: Hana wrote in a homework answer: ‘The opportunity cost of buying bicycles is the price paid for it.’ Explain why this statement is incorrect.
items.answer: Opportunity cost is the next best alternative given up, i.e. what else that money (or resources) could have bought, not the price itself.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: identifies the error; 1 mark: correct explanation – Opportunity cost is the next best alternative given up, i.e. what else that money (or resources) could have bought, not the price itself. [2]

items.stem: Amara can work for 5 hours at $15 an hour or attend a volunteering day, which is free. Amara attends a volunteering day. Calculate the opportunity cost in money terms.
items.markingKey: Forgone wages $15 × 5 = $75 = $75.

items.stem: A farmer in Dravonia can use a field to grow either 150 crates of tea or 90 tonnes of wheat in a season (or any combination at a constant rate). Calculate the opportunity cost of producing one tonne of wheat.
items.answer: 1.67 crates of tea
items.markingKey: 150/90 = 1.67 crates of tea per tonne of wheat.

items.stem: Ana values three ways of spending Saturday: a computer course (worth $75 to Ana); a football coaching job (worth $150 to Ana); a weekend trip (worth $120 to Ana). Ana makes the rational choice. (a) Identify the choice made and calculate its opportunity cost. (b) Explain why the opportunity cost is not $195.
items.answer: (a) a football coaching job; opportunity cost = a weekend trip, worth $120. (b) Only the next best alternative is forgone; Ana could not have done both of the others at once.
items.markingKey: (a) highest value option chosen [1]; opportunity cost = next best, $120 [1] [2] (b) only next best alternative counts [1] [1] Total [3]

items.stem: Extract: The government of Jovania has $1200 million for new projects this year. Ministers have proposed a hospital ($350 million), a rail link to Hanoi ($250 million) and a programme of school building ($150 million), as well as a cut in taxes. Opposition politicians say the government should “stop wasting money and simply do everything”. (a) Calculate how much of the budget would be left if all three projects were funded. (b) Explain the opportunity cost to the government of choosing the rail link.
items.answer: (a) $450 million (b) The benefits of the next best project that cannot now be funded (e.g. the hospital) are forgone.
items.markingKey: (a) 350 + 250 + 150 = 750; |750 − 1200| = 450 [2] (b) 1 mark: next best alternative; 1 mark: applied to extract [2]

items.stem: The government of Zentara must choose between building a new port and expanding free healthcare. Consider whether opportunity cost is the most useful concept for governments when deciding how to spend public money.
items.answer: For: Makes the trade-off explicit; focuses on real alternatives; prevents waste; links to the PPC. Against: Hard to measure non-market benefits; equity and political objectives also matter; information and time constraints; long-term effects uncertain. Conclusion: a reasoned judgement on when the claim holds.
items.markingKey: Analysis (AO1/AO2, up to 8): Makes the trade-off explicit; focuses on real alternatives; prevents waste; links to the PPC. Evaluation (AO3, up to 4): Hard to measure non-market benefits; equity and political objectives also matter; information and time constraints; long-term effects uncertain. Top marks need balanced analysis of both sides and a justified conclusion that answers the question set, explaining what the outcome depends on [12]

items.stem: Which question is about for whom to produce?
options: How many workers should be employed?
Who should receive the goods and services that are produced?
items.answer: Who should receive the goods and services that are produced?
items.markingKey: For whom = distribution of output between people.

items.stem: Explain how the question “for whom to produce?” is linked to the distribution of income.
items.answer: In a market system goods go to those with income to pay for them, so the distribution of income largely determines who receives output; governments may redistribute to change this.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: goods go to those able to pay; 1 mark: income distribution determines allocation/role of redistribution [2]

items.stem: Ironleaf borrows to buy new machines and expand output of rice. Which economic agent is described?
items.answer: Firm
items.markingKey: Firm: it invests in capital and produces output for sale.

items.stem: A farm in Tarvia switches from hand-picking crops to using harvesting machines. Which basic economic question is being answered? Explain your answer.
items.answer: How to produce: it is a change in the method of production / factor combination.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: How to produce; 1 mark: explanation – it is a change in the method of production / factor combination. [2]

items.stem: Daniel, an economics student in Riyadh, is preparing for a class debate on this topic. (a) Explain the three basic economic questions that every economy has to answer. (b) ‘The question of for whom to produce is best left to the market in Loristan.’ Discuss this statement.
items.answer: (a) What, how and for whom to produce; arise from scarcity; examples; different systems answer them differently (price mechanism vs planning). (b) For: Prices reward effort and ration efficiently; consumer sovereignty; incentives to work. Against: Market allocation depends on income, so the poor may lack necessities; merit goods underconsumed; need for redistribution and government provision. Conclusion: a reasoned judgement on when the claim holds.
items.markingKey: (a) Indicative content: What, how and for whom to produce; arise from scarcity; examples; different systems answer them differently (price mechanism vs planning). Level 3 (6–8): accurate knowledge with a clear, developed analytical chain and, where relevant, an accurate, labelled diagram that is used in the answer; Level 2 (3–5): some correct explanation but undeveloped or partly inaccurate; Level 1 (1–2): limited knowledge, mostly assertion [8] (b) Analysis (AO1/AO2, up to 8): Prices reward effort and ration efficiently; consumer sovereignty; incentives to work. Evaluation (AO3, up to 4): Market allocation depends on income, so the poor may lack necessities; merit goods underconsumed; need for redistribution and government provision. Top marks need balanced analysis of both sides and a justified conclusion that answers the question set, explaining what the outcome depends on [12]

items.stem: Which of these is a need rather than a want?
items.answer: Clean drinking water
items.markingKey: Needs are essential for survival (food, water, shelter, clothing); wants are desires beyond these.

items.stem: During a class discussion Zara said: ‘Healthcare in Sundara is free at the point of use, so it is no longer scarce.’ Explain what is wrong with this claim.
items.answer: Healthcare still uses scarce resources (doctors, equipment, buildings) that have alternative uses; a zero price does not remove scarcity, it just changes how the good is rationed.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: identifies the error; 1 mark: correct explanation – Healthcare still uses scarce resources (doctors, equipment, buildings) that have alternative uses; a zero price does not remove scarcity, it just changes how the good is rationed. [2]

items.stem: A student, Noah, claims: ‘High-income countries such as Selmaria do not face the economic problem because they have plenty of money.’ Explain why this statement is incorrect.
items.answer: Money is not a resource for production; all countries have finite land, labour, capital and enterprise relative to unlimited wants, so all face the economic problem.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: identifies the error; 1 mark: correct explanation – Money is not a resource for production; all countries have finite land, labour, capital and enterprise relative to unlimited wants, so all face the economic problem. [2]

items.stem: In Nordavia there are 600 hospital beds but 840 patients needing a bed each night. Calculate the shortfall as a percentage of what is wanted.
Juniper Brands has one factory in Toronto and orders for both bottled water and smartphones that exceed what it can produce. Explain how the basic economic problem applies to Juniper Brands.
items.answer: The factory’s capacity (machines, workers, time) is limited while orders are greater, so Juniper Brands must choose which product to make and in what quantity.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: limited capacity/resources; 1 mark: demand exceeds capacity; 1 mark: choice of what to produce [3]

items.stem: Extract: The government of Kestria has $600 million for new projects this year. Ministers have proposed a hospital ($250 million), a rail link to Jakarta ($350 million) and a programme of school building ($200 million), as well as a cut in taxes. Opposition politicians say the government should “stop wasting money and simply do everything”. (a) Calculate how much more than the budget would be needed to fund all three projects. (b) Explain the opportunity cost to the government of choosing the rail link. (c) Discuss how the government should decide which project to fund.
items.answer: (a) $200 million (b) The benefits of the next best project that cannot now be funded (e.g. the hospital) are forgone. (c) Compare benefits and opportunity costs; consider who gains (for whom), long-run effects on growth, equity and public opinion; data may be uncertain; judgement.
items.markingKey: (a) 250 + 350 + 200 = 800; |800 − 600| = 200 [2] (b) 1 mark: next best alternative; 1 mark: applied to extract [2] (c) 2 marks: analysis of criteria; 2 marks: evaluation and conclusion [4]

items.stem: Why do economists measure opportunity cost in terms of goods forgone rather than money?
options: Because money is only a claim on resources; the real cost is the alternative use of those resources
items.answer: Because money is only a claim on resources; the real cost is the alternative use of those resources
items.markingKey: Opportunity cost is the real sacrifice of alternatives.

items.stem: During a class discussion Felix said: ‘Free school meals in Sundara have no opportunity cost because pupils do not pay.’ Identify what is wrong with this reasoning and give the correct explanation.
items.answer: The meals still use scarce resources that could have produced something else, so society bears an opportunity cost even though pupils pay nothing.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: identifies the error; 1 mark: correct explanation – The meals still use scarce resources that could have produced something else, so society bears an opportunity cost even though pupils pay nothing. [2]

items.stem: Yusuf makes the following statement: ‘Free school meals in Loristan have no opportunity cost because pupils do not pay.’ Identify the error in this statement and correct it.
items.answer: The meals still use scarce resources that could have produced something else, so society bears an opportunity cost even though pupils pay nothing.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: identifies the error; 1 mark: correct explanation – The meals still use scarce resources that could have produced something else, so society bears an opportunity cost even though pupils pay nothing. [2]

items.stem: Fenwick & Co uses its factory to make chocolate bars instead of paper. Explain the opportunity cost to Fenwick & Co.
items.answer: The profit (or output) from making paper, the next best use of the factory, is given up.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: forgone output/profit of cinema tickets; 1 mark: next best use of the resources [2]

items.stem: Tomás can work for 5 hours at $10 an hour or attend a music festival, which costs $20 to enter. Tomás attends a music festival. Calculate the opportunity cost of attending, measured in money.
items.markingKey: Forgone wages $10 × 5 = $50 + entry fee $20 = $70.

items.stem: A farmer in Dravonia can use a field to grow either 120 crates of tea or 40 bales of cotton in a season (or any combination at a constant rate). Calculate the opportunity cost of producing one bale of cotton.
items.answer: 3 crates of tea
items.markingKey: 120/40 = 3 crates of tea per bale of cotton.

items.stem: Felix values three ways of spending Saturday: a private tutoring session (worth $60 to Felix); a part-time job (worth $150 to Felix); a weekend trip (worth $140 to Felix). Felix makes the rational choice. (a) Identify the choice made and calculate its opportunity cost. (b) Explain why the opportunity cost is not $200.
items.answer: (a) a part-time job; opportunity cost = a weekend trip, worth $140. (b) Only the next best alternative is forgone; Felix could not have done both of the others at once.
items.markingKey: (a) highest value option chosen [1]; opportunity cost = next best, $140 [1] [2] (b) only next best alternative counts [1] [1] Total [3]

items.stem: Extract: The government of Nordavia has $800 million for new projects this year. Ministers have proposed a hospital ($200 million), a rail link to Kathmandu ($150 million) and a programme of school building ($300 million), as well as a cut in taxes. Opposition politicians say the government should “stop wasting money and simply do everything”. (a) Calculate how much of the budget would be left if all three projects were funded. (b) Explain the opportunity cost to the government of choosing the rail link.
items.answer: (a) $150 million (b) The benefits of the next best project that cannot now be funded (e.g. the hospital) are forgone.
items.markingKey: (a) 200 + 150 + 300 = 650; |650 − 800| = 150 [2] (b) 1 mark: next best alternative; 1 mark: applied to extract [2]

items.stem: Extract: The government of Fendaria has $1200 million for new projects this year. Ministers have proposed a hospital ($300 million), a rail link to Toronto ($250 million) and a programme of school building ($150 million), as well as a cut in taxes. Opposition politicians say the government should “stop wasting money and simply do everything”. (a) Calculate how much of the budget would be left if all three projects were funded. (b) Using the extract, explain the meaning of the basic economic problem. (c) Explain the opportunity cost to the government of choosing the rail link. (d) Explain why the opposition’s suggestion to “do everything” does not solve the economic problem. (e) Discuss how the government should decide which project to fund.
items.answer: (a) $500 million (b) Limited resources (a budget of $1200 million) but many competing wants (hospital, rail, schools, tax cuts), so choices must be made. (c) The benefits of the next best project that cannot now be funded (e.g. the hospital) are forgone. (d) Borrowing or taxing more still uses scarce resources; resources diverted from private uses or future spending have an opportunity cost. (e) Compare benefits and opportunity costs; consider who gains (for whom), long-run effects on growth, equity and public opinion; data may be uncertain; judgement.
items.markingKey: (a) 300 + 250 + 150 = 700; |700 − 1200| = 500 [2] (b) 1 mark: limited resources; 1 mark: unlimited/competing wants; 1 mark: use of extract [3] (c) 1 mark: next best alternative; 1 mark: applied to extract [2] (d) 1 mark: resources still finite; 1 mark: cost moves elsewhere/future [2] (e) 2 marks: analysis of criteria; 2 marks: evaluation and conclusion [4]

items.stem: Why must every economy answer the questions of what, how and for whom to produce?
options: Because firms aim to maximise profit
Because resources are scarce and have alternative uses
items.answer: Because resources are scarce and have alternative uses
items.markingKey: Scarcity forces choices about resource allocation.

items.stem: Korvia introduces free school meals for children from low-income families. Identify which basic economic question this addresses and explain why.
items.answer: For whom to produce: it determines who receives the output (low-income children) regardless of ability to pay.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: for whom; 1 mark: distribution explained [2]

items.stem: Lumen Ltd decides to use solar power rather than diesel generators in its factory in Doha. Which basic economic question is being answered?
items.answer: How to produce
items.markingKey: How to produce: it chooses the technique and inputs used in production.

items.stem: Zara works 35 hours a week and spends the wage on food and rent. Which economic agent is described? Explain your answer.
items.answer: Household: supplies labour and buys goods and services to maximise utility.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: Household; 1 mark: explanation – supplies labour and buys goods and services to maximise utility. [2]

items.stem: Kwame, an economics student in Seoul, is preparing for a class debate on this topic. (a) Explain the three basic economic questions that every economy has to answer. (b) Assess the extent to which the question of for whom to produce is best left to the market in Ostrelia.
items.answer: (a) What, how and for whom to produce; arise from scarcity; examples; different systems answer them differently (price mechanism vs planning). (b) For: Prices reward effort and ration efficiently; consumer sovereignty; incentives to work. Against: Market allocation depends on income, so the poor may lack necessities; merit goods underconsumed; need for redistribution and government provision. Conclusion: a reasoned judgement on when the claim holds.
items.markingKey: (a) Indicative content: What, how and for whom to produce; arise from scarcity; examples; different systems answer them differently (price mechanism vs planning). Level 3 (6–8): accurate knowledge with a clear, developed analytical chain and, where relevant, an accurate, labelled diagram that is used in the answer; Level 2 (3–5): some correct explanation but undeveloped or partly inaccurate; Level 1 (1–2): limited knowledge, mostly assertion [8] (b) Analysis (AO1/AO2, up to 8): Prices reward effort and ration efficiently; consumer sovereignty; incentives to work. Evaluation (AO3, up to 4): Market allocation depends on income, so the poor may lack necessities; merit goods underconsumed; need for redistribution and government provision. Top marks need balanced analysis of both sides and a justified conclusion that answers the question set, explaining what the outcome depends on [12]
